AI Marketing Foundations: Tools, Prompts and Brand Voice

This module shows you what AI writing and image tools actually do, where they help a marketer and where they cause harm. You will learn to write a complete marketing prompt brief and build a brand voice guide that keeps every AI draft sounding like your brand, not like a robot.

Tools such as **ChatGPT**, **Google Gemini**, **Microsoft Copilot**, **Claude** and **Meta AI** (inside WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook) are built on **large language models**, often shortened to LLMs. An LLM has learned patterns from a huge amount of text. When you type a request, it predicts, word by word, the text that most likely fits. It does not look up a truth table, and it does not know your business unless you tell it. That single fact explains both why these tools are useful and why they go wrong.

What AI is genuinely good at for marketers
**Variation:** twenty headline options, five versions of a caption, three email subject lines to test.
**Reshaping:** turning one long product description into a WhatsApp Status line, an Instagram caption and an email paragraph.
**First drafts and outlines:** a blog outline, a campaign plan skeleton, a FAQ list from customer questions you paste in.
**Summarising:** condensing 40 customer reviews into the five most common praises and complaints.
**Image ideas and simple graphics:** tools such as Canva's AI features, Adobe Firefly or Meta AI can produce concept images you then check carefully.

A useful rule: **AI drafts, you decide.** The tool can save time on the mechanical parts of marketing, but the strategy, the facts, the final words and the responsibility stay with you. If a customer is misled by a post, 'the AI wrote it' is not a defence.
Three kinds of marketing work

Before you use any tool, sort your work. **AI-assisted** tasks are ones where AI produces a draft and you edit: captions, ad variations, outlines. **Automated** tasks run without you each time once set up, using features built into platforms: a WhatsApp Business greeting message, a scheduled Facebook post, a welcome email sent when someone joins your list. **Human-led** tasks need your judgement every time: choosing which product to promote, replying to an angry customer, setting prices, approving claims.

Worked example: a weekly task audit

For example, Ngozi handles marketing for a small catering business in Ibadan. She writes down how she spent her marketing time in one normal week, then tries AI support and platform automation for two weeks and notes the new times.
Captions for 6 Instagram and Facebook posts: 4 hours before. With an AI first draft that she edits: 2 hours. Saved 2 hours.
Answering repeated WhatsApp questions (menu, prices, delivery areas): 6 hours before. With WhatsApp Business quick replies she wrote once: 4.5 hours. Saved 1.5 hours.
Monthly report for the owner, spread over the month: 2 hours a week before. With AI summarising her figures, which she then checks: 1 hour. Saved 1 hour.
Designing graphics: 3 hours. No change, because she already uses Canva templates.
Planning next week's offers with the owner: 1 hour. No change, this is human-led.
Total before: 4 + 6 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 16 hours. Total after: 2 + 4.5 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 11.5 hours.
Ngozi saves 4.5 hours a week (16 minus 11.5). She decides to spend 2 of those hours replying personally to bigger catering enquiries, the work that brings most of the money.
Protect customer data

Do not paste customer names, phone numbers, addresses or payment details into a public AI chat tool. Many tools may use what you type to improve their systems unless you change the data settings. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires you to handle personal data lawfully and securely. Replace names with codes such as C001 before asking AI for help.

Free versions of most AI chat tools are enough for this course. Paid plans usually add longer conversations, file uploads or newer models, but they do not remove the need to check every draft. Ask for options, not one answer

One draft forces you to accept or reject. Ten drafts let you compare. Ask for variations that differ in a named way, for example 'give me 8 headlines: 2 that lead with price, 2 with convenience, 2 with a question, 2 with a customer result'. This also shows you which angle the tool handles best.

Then score the options. Use three criteria that matter for the piece, each from 1 to 5. For a headline: **Clarity** (does a stranger understand the offer in two seconds?), **Benefit** (is the reason to care obvious?) and **Voice** (does it sound like the brand?). Add the scores. The highest total goes forward, but you may still combine the best parts of two options.
Worked example: from thin prompt to tested headline

For example, Amaka sells unrefined shea butter in Abuja through Instagram and WhatsApp. Her first prompt, 'write a headline for my shea butter', gave 'Unlock the Secret to Radiant Skin!', which sounds like every other brand and hints at a claim she cannot prove.

She rewrites the request with role, audience (busy mothers), offer (200 g tub, free delivery in Wuse until Friday), format (headline under 10 words), voice (warm, practical) and constraints (no medical or 'secret' claims).
She asks for 6 headlines: 2 on convenience, 2 on the family use, 2 as questions.

She scores three favourites on Clarity, Benefit and Voice (1 to 5 each). 'One tub for the whole family's dry skin': 5 + 4 + 5 = 14. 'Dry elbows? We deliver to Wuse free this week': 4 + 5 + 4 = 13. 'Pure shea, nothing added': 4 + 3 + 4 = 11.
She follows up: 'Keep option 1, add the free delivery in Wuse, stay under 12 words.'
The tool returns 'One tub for the whole family's dry skin. Free Wuse delivery this week.' She checks: the tub size, the delivery area and the deadline are all true.
A specific, honest headline in about 10 minutes, and a saved prompt she can reuse for every new promotion by changing only the offer line.

Build a prompt library

Keep a Google Doc or Notes file called 'Prompt library'. For each prompt that worked, save the full brief, the date, the tool you used and one line on the result. After a month you will have tested templates for captions, ads, emails and reports, and anyone on your team can use them.

Different tools will give different results from the same brief, and the same tool can give a different answer each time you ask. That is normal. If you need consistency, keep the brief and the examples the same, and judge the output with the same scoring table every time.

Start a fresh conversation for each new task. In a very long chat, earlier instructions can be given less weight and details from an old task can leak into the new one. Paste your brief and voice guide again at the top of each new chat: it takes seconds and keeps results steady.

When many people, or many AI drafts, speak for one brand, the brand starts to sound like strangers. A **brand voice guide** is a short document that describes how the brand speaks, with clear examples. A good one helps a new team member, a freelancer and an AI tool produce copy that sounds like the same person. Keep it to two pages: if it is longer, nobody will use it, including you.

Word bank and banned list

Your **word bank** holds words and phrases your customers actually use and that you want repeated: product names, local terms, your sign-off. Your **banned list** holds words the brand never uses, either because they sound wrong or because they are risky. For a skincare or food brand, words that suggest a medical effect, such as 'cures', 'treats eczema' or 'heals', are banned unless the product is registered and approved for that claim. 'Organic' and 'NAFDAC approved' are banned unless you can show the certificate or registration number.
Using the guide with AI
Paste the whole guide at the start of a conversation, or save it in a feature that remembers instructions, such as custom instructions in ChatGPT or a Gem in Gemini, where available on your plan.
Add two or three real sample posts and say: 'Match the voice of these examples.' Examples teach style better than descriptions.
Write your request using the prompt brief from Lesson 1.2.
Ask the tool to check its own draft: 'List any words from the banned list or any claims from the never list in this draft.'
Edit by hand. The guide reduces editing; it does not remove it.
Worked example: testing whether AI matches the voice
For example, Zainab runs an adire studio in Abeokuta. She writes a voice guide (warm, proud of craft, plain) and wants to know if AI drafts now sound like her.
She asks an AI tool for 4 Instagram captions for a new indigo wrapper, giving it her guide and 3 of her past captions.
She mixes the 4 AI captions (edited only for facts) with 4 captions she wrote herself last year, numbers them 1 to 8 and removes any dates.
She asks two loyal customers on WhatsApp to mark which captions 'sound like Zainab'.
Customer A marks 6 of 8, customer B marks 5 of 8. Of the 11 'sounds like Zainab' marks, 5 went to AI captions and 6 to her own.
One AI caption got no marks. She sees it used 'elevate your wardrobe', adds 'elevate' to her banned list and reruns.
5 of 11 marks (about 45%) went to AI drafts, close to half, so the guide is working. The one failure shows her exactly which phrase to ban.
Write the guide yourself first

You can ask AI to suggest voice traits from your past posts, but decide the final traits yourself. A voice guide written entirely by AI tends to describe the average brand, which is the opposite of what you want.

Review the guide every three months. Add phrases customers repeat back to you in messages, remove words that feel tired, and add any new claim you are now allowed to make, such as a NAFDAC registration number once it is granted. Store the guide where the whole team can find it, for example a pinned Google Doc.

Do not forget the **formatting habits** section. Write down how the brand handles emojis (for example, at most two per post), hashtags (three to five, always including the brand tag), capital letters (never whole words in capitals), prices (always written in full as ₦5,000, never '5k') and the sign-off. These small habits are exactly what AI drafts get wrong, and they are easy to state as rules.
Pidgin and Nigerian languages

If your brand mixes English with Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa or Igbo, put real examples in the guide. AI tools often produce stiff or wrong phrasing in Nigerian languages and Pidgin. Always have a fluent speaker check any line in a local language before it is published.

A campaign is a set of messages with one goal and one deadline. The common mistake with AI is to ask for each piece separately, so the WhatsApp message promises one thing, the Instagram caption another and the email a third. The fix is to write a **core message** first, by yourself, and make AI adapt it. Everything is then consistent, and AI does the slow part: reshaping the same idea for each channel.
The core message sheet
**Goal:** one measurable result, for example 40 Christmas cake orders.
**Offer:** what, price, how to order, deadline.
**Audience:** who, and the one thing they worry about (for example, 'will the cake arrive on time?').
**Proof:** real things you can show: photos of past cakes, genuine reviews with permission, years in business.
**Call to action:** one clear next step, such as 'Send CAKE on WhatsApp'.
**Never say:** risky words and claims from your voice guide.

Worked example: testing three AI ad texts

For example, Blessing runs a home bakery in Port Harcourt. Her goal is 40 Christmas cake orders. She sets aside about ₦15,000 (approximate) for a Facebook and Instagram ad and asks AI for three primary texts from her core message.

Text A, price-led: 'Moist fruit cake, 1 kg, order by 20 December.' Text B, worry-led: 'No last-minute cake panic. Order now, delivered on the day you choose.' Text C, proof-led: 'Our customers reorder every year. See last year's cakes.'
She uses the A/B test option in Meta Ads Manager so each text gets a fair, separate share of the budget: ₦5,000 each.
Results after 5 days: A gets 120 link clicks, B gets 200, C gets 80.
She checks orders too: the clicks from B led to 9 orders, from A to 5, from C to 2.
Text B, the worry-led message, wins on both cost per click (₦25) and orders (9). She moves the remaining budget to B and uses its 'no panic' angle in her WhatsApp Status and email.

Decide how you will know where each order came from **before** you launch. A simple method that works with WhatsApp selling: give each channel its own order word, for example 'CAKE-IG' in Instagram posts, 'CAKE-FB' in the ad and 'CAKE-EM' in the email. When a customer sends the word, label the chat in WhatsApp Business. At the end of the campaign, count the labels and you know which channel brought real orders, not just likes.
Change one thing at a time

If text, image and audience all differ between ads, you cannot know which change made the difference. Keep the same image and audience and test only the text, or keep the text and test only the image.
Schedule, then step back

Once posts are approved, schedule them in **Meta Business Suite** (Planner) for Facebook and Instagram, and in your email tool for the email. Scheduling is the simplest form of automation: it removes the daily rush and the risk of forgetting. WhatsApp Status cannot be scheduled inside the WhatsApp Business app, so set a phone reminder.
AI images in ads

If you use an AI-generated image of a product, it must show what the customer will really receive. A perfect AI cake that looks nothing like your cake is misleading. Use real product photos for anything a customer is buying, and check each platform's current rules on labelling AI-made images.

Sending the same message to every customer wastes money and annoys people. A customer who bought yesterday does not need a 'we miss you' discount, and a loyal customer who has gone quiet deserves more than a general broadcast. **Segmentation** means grouping customers by behaviour so each group gets a message that fits. A simple, well-known method is **RFM**: Recency, Frequency and Monetary value.

For example, Funke sells home-made spices and pepper mixes in Lagos through WhatsApp. She scores 8 customers with the thresholds above (spend figures are her own records).

Consent and data protection

Message only people who agreed to hear from you, and make it easy to say stop. WhatsApp broadcasts only reach contacts who saved your number. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis for using personal data, security for the data you keep and respect for people who ask you to stop. Never upload a customer list with names and numbers to a public AI tool.

Re-score every month. Customers move between segments, and the movement is itself useful: if more customers drift from Steady to At risk this month, something has changed, perhaps a price rise or a slow delivery, and that is a question for you, not for AI.

AI tools are also useful helpers inside the sheet itself. You can describe a problem, for example 'my IFS formula returns an error when the date cell is empty', and ask for a fix, without sharing any customer data. Be careful with small numbers, though: with only 20 customers, one person moving segment changes the percentages a lot, so look at the actual customers on your private code list, not only at the totals.

A report needs correct numbers and a clear story. AI is good at the story and unreliable at the numbers: it can make arithmetic slips or mix up figures. So calculate in Google Sheets first, then paste the finished numbers and ask AI to write a short summary for the owner, in plain language, with three recommendations. Check that every number in its summary matches your sheet.
**Click rate on reach** = link clicks ÷ accounts reached × 100.
**Chat-to-order rate** = orders ÷ new WhatsApp chats × 100.
**Average order value** = revenue ÷ number of orders.
**Change** = (this week − last week) ÷ last week × 100.
Worked example: a weekly report with checked numbers
For example, Chioma manages marketing for a small fashion accessories shop in Enugu. She pulls figures from Instagram Insights, WhatsApp chats and her sales book.
Last week: reach 3,500, link clicks 105, new chats 40, orders 8, revenue ₦56,000.
This week: reach 4,200, link clicks 168, new chats 52, orders 13, revenue ₦97,500.
Click rate: 105 ÷ 3,500 = 3.0% last week; 168 ÷ 4,200 = 4.0% this week.
Chat-to-order: 8 ÷ 40 = 20% last week; 13 ÷ 52 = 25% this week.
Revenue change: (97,500 − 56,000) ÷ 56,000 × 100 = about 74%. She pastes these finished numbers into AI and asks for a 120-word summary with three recommendations.
The AI summary first says revenue rose '64%'. Chioma catches it against her sheet, corrects it to 74% and sends the owner a report she can trust.

When you produce more content, you also produce more chances to be wrong. One wrong price, a copied competitor slogan or an unproven health claim can cost more than all the time AI saved. **Quality control** is the routine that catches these problems before customers see them. Claims and the rules behind them

In Nigeria, advertising is regulated by the **Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON)**, and some adverts need its approval before they are published. The **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)** deals with misleading claims to consumers. **NAFDAC** controls regulated products such as food, drinks and cosmetics, including what may be said about them. You do not need to be a lawyer, but you must know that 'AI wrote it' changes nothing: the business that publishes a claim is responsible for it. When a campaign is large or the product is regulated, check the current requirements with the relevant body before publishing.

The AI use log

Keep a simple Google Sheet with one row per published piece: date, channel, tool used, prompt link (from your prompt library), what you changed, who approved, and any issue found. It takes a minute per piece. It protects you when a client asks 'did AI write this?', helps you spot which prompts need the most fixing, and becomes proof of your process for your portfolio.
Worked example: checking a batch of ten drafts
For example, Halima produces a week of content for a client's pharmacy-adjacent wellness shop in Kaduna: 10 AI-assisted pieces (6 posts, 3 WhatsApp Status sets and 1 email).
She runs the six-point check at about 3 minutes per piece: 10 × 3 = 30 minutes.
Piece 2 says a herbal tea 'boosts immunity and prevents malaria'. Check 2 fails: an unprovable health claim on a regulated product. She rewrites it to describe taste, ingredients and how to brew it.
Piece 5 lists the price as ₦4,500; the client's price list says ₦5,000. Check 1 fails. Corrected.
Piece 8 includes a 'customer review' the AI invented. Check 6 fails. She replaces it with a real review the client has permission to share.
The other 7 pass. She logs all 10, noting the 3 issues and which prompts produced them.

3 of 10 pieces (30%) needed fixing, including one that could have caused serious harm. Half an hour of checking protected the client. Halima updates the prompt to say 'no health benefit claims, no reviews unless I paste them'.
Should you tell people AI was used?

Agree the answer with each client in writing. Many businesses are open about using AI for drafting while making clear that people check and approve everything. Platforms may require labels on realistic AI-generated images or video, so check their current rules. Never present an AI-generated person as a real customer.
Review your log monthly. If one type of piece keeps failing the same check, fix the cause, usually the prompt or the voice guide, rather than fixing the same mistake every week.
Checking AI images

AI images need their own close look. Zoom in on hands, faces and any text inside the picture: AI often adds extra fingers, warped faces or spelling that looks like words but is not. Look for logos or packaging that resemble a real brand. Ask whether the image could make a customer expect something you do not sell. If any answer worries you, use a real photo instead. A plain, honest phone photo of your actual product is safer than a perfect image of something that does not exist.

Finally, use a second pair of eyes for anything high-stakes: a paid campaign, a price change, a product launch or any health, money or safety topic. The person who wrote or prompted a piece reads what she meant to write, not what is on the screen. A colleague, the client or even a trusted friend will spot errors you cannot.

Worked example: pricing a setup project

For example, Esther is a freelance marketer in Abuja quoting a setup project for a small restaurant. Her own target rate is ₦8,000 per hour (an illustrative figure; set your own from your costs and local market).

She estimates hours: voice guide 6, prompt library of 10 tested prompts 5, WhatsApp automations and quick replies 3, four-email welcome sequence 6, handover training 3. Total: 6 + 5 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 23 hours.
She adds a 15% buffer for meetings and revisions: 23 × 1.15 = 26.45, rounded to 26.5 hours.
She states exclusions: ad spend and any paid tool subscriptions are paid directly by the client.
She asks for 50% (₦106,000) before starting and 50% on handover.
A clear quote of ₦212,000 for named deliverables. If AI helps her finish in 20 hours, the client still receives exactly what was agreed and Esther earns more per hour.
Scope terms that protect both sides
**Revisions:** for example, two rounds of changes per deliverable; more rounds are quoted separately.
**Inputs:** the client supplies photos, prices and approvals by agreed dates; delays move the deadline.
**Accounts:** the client owns their WhatsApp, Meta and email accounts. You are added as a user, never the owner, and access is removed at the end.
**AI use:** state that AI tools assist drafting and that all content is checked by you and approved by the client.
**Change requests:** new work outside the list is quoted in writing before you start.
Do not sell hours saved
Avoid promising 'AI will double your sales'. You cannot prove it in advance. Promise deliverables and a measurement plan instead, such as a weekly report on chats, orders and cost per click.
Pricing a monthly retainer

For a retainer, list the monthly quantities clearly, for example 12 feed posts, 8 WhatsApp Status sets, 4 emails and 4 weekly reports, plus the turnaround time for approvals. Estimate your hours per item from your AI use log, not from guesswork: if a checked post takes you 25 minutes on average, 12 posts take 300 minutes, which is 5 hours. Add the hours for every item, add a buffer for meetings, multiply by your rate, and review the price after three months when you have real figures.

If you pay for an AI tool or a scheduling tool and use it for several clients, treat the subscription as a business overhead and build it into your hourly rate. If a client needs a tool only for their own work, such as a larger email plan, the client should hold and pay for that account directly.
**Red flag:** the client wants '100 posts a month' with no approval person. Agree a smaller number and a named approver.
**Red flag:** the client asks you to invent reviews or 'make the product sound like it cures things'. Decline that part in writing.
**Red flag:** no access to past sales or customer records. Start with a setup project and a tracking sheet before promising results.

How AI really works
It predicts words. It does not know you.
Predicts likely text, word by word
Does not know your business
Great at variation and first drafts
The facts and the decision stay with you
Tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI are built on large language models, or LLMs. An LLM predicts, word by word, the text that most likely fits your request.
It does not look up the truth, and it does not know your business unless you tell it. That one fact explains why it helps, and why it goes wrong.
It is strong at variation, reshaping one text for many channels, first drafts and summaries.
But the strategy, the facts, the final words and the responsibility stay with you. If a customer is misled, the AI wrote it is not a defence.
Watch for these
Invented facts and claims
First, invented facts. A caption may claim your soap is dermatologist approved. Never publish a claim, number, price or quote you cannot prove yourself.
Second, outdated information, like an old price or an old platform feature. Check before posting.
Third, generic tone. Every post starts to sound the same.
Fourth, bias. Images may show only one skin tone or body type. Review everything with your real customers in mind.

Step by step
Write a full prompt brief
Check every fact before you publish.
Role, audience and offer
Format and voice
Constraints: what must not appear
One or two past posts as examples
Ask for named variations, then score
Thin prompts give average copy. Write a brief like you would for a human copywriter. Start with the role, the audience and the offer.
Then the format, such as an Instagram caption under 80 words, and the voice.
Then constraints: no medical claims, no cures, no invented reviews.
Paste one or two past posts that worked. Examples teach style better than adjectives.
Ask for options that differ in a named way, then score your favourites on clarity, benefit and voice, from 1 to 5 each.
For example, Amaka sells shea butter in Abuja. Her winning headline scored 14. She refines it with short follow-ups, then checks that the tub size, delivery area and deadline are all true.
Brand voice
Define each trait: this, not that
Warm like a trusted older sister
Names the technique
Short sentences, prices stated
Hey babe!!!
Exquisite premium elegance
DM for price on every post

A brand voice guide keeps every draft sounding like one person. Keep it to two pages. Choose three traits, and define each with this, not that, because adjectives alone mean different things to different people.
Warm does not mean over-familiar. Proud of craft does not mean empty luxury words. Plain means prices are stated, not hidden.
Stay safe and legal
Banned claims and private data
No cures, heals or treats eczema
No organic without a certificate
No NAFDAC approved without registration
Customer names replaced with codes
Local-language lines checked by a speaker

Put risky words on your banned list. Medical claims such as cures or heals are banned unless the product is approved for that claim. Organic and NAFDAC approved are banned unless you can show the certificate or registration number.
Never paste customer names, phone numbers or payment details into a public AI chat. Replace names with codes, as the Data Protection Act 2023 requires careful handling.
And have a fluent speaker check any Pidgin or local-language line.

Step by step
One core message, many channels
You write the core message. AI only adapts it.
Write the core message sheet yourself
AI adapts it for each channel
Edit and check every price and date

The common mistake is asking AI for each piece separately. Then WhatsApp promises one thing and Instagram another. So first, write a core message sheet yourself: the goal, the offer, the audience, real proof and one call to action.
Then paste it with your voice guide and ask AI to adapt it. Four short WhatsApp Status slides. An Instagram caption with the hook in the first 8 words. An email with 5 subject lines.
Edit every draft. AI sometimes improves a detail, changing order by 20 December into order by Christmas.
Then schedule posts in Meta Business Suite, and measure.
The message and the facts are yours. AI does the slow reshaping.
Worked example
Blessing tests three ad texts
For example, Blessing runs a home bakery in Port Harcourt and wants 40 Christmas cake orders.
Budget for each text
Price-led: cost per click
Worry-led: cost per click
Proof-led: cost per click
Naira amounts are approximate.
Here is a fair test. Blessing sets aside about 15,000 naira and asks AI for three ad texts: one led by price, one by worry, one by proof.
She uses the A/B test option in Meta Ads Manager, so each text gets a fair 5,000 naira. The image and audience stay the same. Only the text changes.
After 5 days, the price-led text costs about 42 naira a click. The worry-led text, no last-minute cake panic, costs 25 naira. The proof-led text costs about 63.
She checks orders too, not just clicks. The worry-led text brought 9 orders, so she moves the rest of her budget there.
Segmentation
Score customers with RFM
Recency: days since last purchase
Frequency: orders in 6 months
Monetary: spend in 6 months
Score each from 1 to 3 in Google Sheets
Sending one message to everyone wastes money and annoys people. Group customers by behaviour with RFM. R is recency, how many days since her last purchase.
F is frequency, how many orders in the last 6 months.
M is monetary, how much she spent in those 6 months.
Score each from 1 to 3 with simple IFS formulas in Google Sheets. Use customer codes such as C001, never names and phone numbers.
Funke's segments, different messages
Recent, frequent, high spend. No discount. Thank them and offer early access to a new blend.
C003 spent well but has not bought for 120 days. Send a personal voice note.
Give a recipe or usage tip so they succeed, instead of a discount.
For example, Funke sells spices in Lagos on WhatsApp. She scores 8 customers. Her champion, C001, needs thanks and early access, not a discount.
C003 is a high spender who has not bought for 120 days. That one customer is worth a personal voice note, not a broadcast.
New customers get a tip on how to use the product. Give AI only the segment descriptions to draft each message, never the customer list. You decide the offers, because only you know your margins.
Protect customers, money
Rules before you automate
Message only people who agreed
Make it easy to say stop
Account details in a quick reply you typed
Never let AI type or change bank details
Complaints always get a person
Automation means a trigger, an action and a regular check by you. Set up your WhatsApp Business greeting, away message and quick replies.
But message only people who agreed, and make stopping easy. Fraudsters copy business names and send fake account numbers, so type your official account details yourself and never let AI change them.
And complaints, refunds and custom orders always get a personal reply.
Chioma checks her weekly report
For example, Chioma manages marketing for a fashion accessories shop in Enugu.
Revenue last week
Revenue this week
Average order, last week
Average order, this week
AI wrote 64%. Her sheet says 74%.
AI is good at the story in a report, and unreliable at the numbers. So calculate in Google Sheets first.
Chioma's revenue rose from 56,000 naira to 97,500 naira. Her sheet says that is about 74% more.
Average order value rose from 7,000 to 7,500 naira, and chats turning into orders rose from 20% to 25%.
She asks AI for a 120-word summary. It says revenue rose 64%. Chioma catches the slip against her sheet and corrects it before the owner sees it.
Key points
Remember
Write the core message; AI adapts it
Test one change at a time; count orders
Different segments, different messages
Never share customer lists with AI
Calculate numbers yourself, then check AI

To remember. Write the core message yourself and let AI adapt it. Test one change at a time, and count real orders. Give each segment its own message. Keep customer lists out of AI tools. And calculate your numbers first, then check every figure AI writes.

Why this matters
Speed only helps if the work is right
One wrong price costs more than time saved
An unproven health claim can cause harm
AI wrote it changes nothing
The publisher is responsible
When you produce more content, you produce more chances to be wrong. One wrong price, a copied slogan or an unproven health claim can cost more than all the time AI saved.

In Nigeria, ARCON regulates advertising, the FCCPC deals with misleading claims, and NAFDAC controls what may be said about food, drinks and cosmetics. Whoever drafted it, the business that publishes a claim is responsible.
Every piece, every time
The six-point quality check
Facts: prices, dates, sizes correct
Claims: can I prove each one?
Voice: no banned words
Rights: not copied from another brand
Respect: realistic, respectful images
Privacy: no invented or unapproved reviews
Run six checks on every AI-assisted piece. One, facts: is every price, date and size correct? Two, claims: can I prove each one with a document, test or record?
Three, voice: does it avoid banned words? Four, rights: is it ours, not too close to a known brand?
Five, respect: would every customer feel respected? Zoom in on AI images for extra fingers and fake text. Six, privacy: no personal data, and no review used without permission.
Worked example
Halima checks ten drafts
A herbal tea that prevents malaria. Unprovable health claim. Rewritten to taste and brewing.
Price written as 4,500 naira. The client's list says 5,000 naira. Corrected.
AI invented a customer review. Replaced with a real one used with permission.

For example, Halima checks 10 pieces for a wellness shop in Kaduna, at about 3 minutes each, so 30 minutes. Piece 2 says a herbal tea prevents malaria. That could cause serious harm, so she rewrites it to describe taste and how to brew it.
Piece 5 lists 4,500 naira, but the price list says 5,000 naira.
Piece 8 has a review the AI invented. 3 of 10 pieces needed fixing. She logs them all in her AI use log and updates her prompt so the mistakes stop at the source.
Approval routine
Separate the person who checks from the one who approves.
AI draft plus your edit
Record it in the AI use log
Make it a routine. You draft with AI and edit, run the six checks, and then the owner or client approves.
Publish, then add a row to your AI use log: date, channel, tool, what you changed and who approved. It takes a minute per piece.
A second pair of eyes catches what the writer cannot, especially for paid campaigns, prices, and anything about health, money or safety.
Esther prices a setup project
For example, Esther is a freelance marketer in Abuja quoting a setup project for a small restaurant.
Her rate per hour
26.5 hours, with 15% buffer
Paid before starting (50%)
Illustrative rate. Set your own.

Now pricing. Package your work as a setup project, a monthly content retainer, or team training. Esther's target rate is 8,000 naira an hour. That is an illustrative figure; set your own from your costs.
She estimates 23 hours for the voice guide, prompt library, WhatsApp automations, welcome emails and handover. She adds a 15% buffer, giving 26.5 hours.
26.5 hours at 8,000 naira is 212,000 naira for named deliverables. If AI helps her finish faster, she earns more per hour.
She asks for 50%, 106,000 naira, before starting and the rest on handover. Ad spend and tool subscriptions are paid by the client directly.
Scope terms
Promise deliverables, not miracles
Put in writing
Two rounds of revisions
Client owns all accounts
You are a user, removed at the end
AI assists; people check and approve
Never promise
AI will double your sales
Invented reviews
Product cures things
100 posts with no approver
Write scope terms that protect both sides. Limit revisions. The client owns their WhatsApp, Meta and email accounts; you are added as a user and removed at the end.

Never promise that AI will double sales, because you cannot prove it in advance. Promise deliverables and a weekly measurement report instead. If a client asks for invented reviews or cure claims, decline that part in writing.
Hauwa reports a result honestly
The numbers
6 orders a week before
9 orders a week during
A 50% rise in 4 weeks
Honest context
December gifting season
Client cut delivery fees
Effects cannot be separated
Finally, prove it honestly. A case study shows the raw AI draft beside your final version, what your checks caught, and the result.
For example, Hauwa, a freelancer in Kano, works 4 weeks for a skincare client. Orders rise from 6 a week to 9 a week. That is a 50% rise.
But it was December, a busy gifting season, and the client also cut delivery fees. Hauwa says so in her case study. A careful client trusts that more than a boast.
Key points
Remember
Six checks on every piece
The publisher owns every claim
Hours plus buffer times your rate
Clients own their accounts
Report results with honest context
To remember. Run the six checks on every piece. The publisher owns every claim. Price from hours, plus a buffer, times your rate. Clients own their accounts. And report results with honest context.
